relationship: Rehoboam’s accession age and Jerusalem reign in parallel notices
rationale: Both give Rehoboam forty-one at accession, seventeen years in Jerusalem and a mother described as Ammonite or Ammanite. Naamah and Noomma remain the supplied forms; the chosen-name city clause is retained without a new dating calculation.

relationship: The two Rehoboam summaries explicitly judge his conduct evil
rationale: Kings says Rehoboam did evil before the Lord and provoked Him; Chronicles says he did evil because he did not direct his heart to seek the Lord. The distinct reasons are retained rather than made identical wording.

relationship: Pillars and groves on high hills and under leafy trees
rationale: Both describe setting up pillars or standing stones and groves on high hills and beneath shady or leafy trees. The source's additional high-place clause and the different regnal settings are not silently transferred between the notices.

relationship: Adopting the removed nations’ abominations beside the stated prohibition
rationale: Kings reports practices from the nations' abominations after their removal; Deuteronomy forbids learning those abominations and gives them as a reason for removal. The source's conspiracy label is not independently translated into a specific cult act.

relationship: Egypt’s king attacks Jerusalem in Rehoboam’s fifth year
rationale: Both date the Egyptian king's Jerusalem campaign to Rehoboam's fifth year. Shishak and Sousakim remain the actual personal forms, and Chronicles' stated reason is not added to Kings' short campaign notice.

relationship: Lord-house and royal-house treasures and gold shields are taken
rationale: Both report taking the treasures of the Lord's and king's houses and gold shields. Kings additionally describes David's captured golden spears, whereas Chronicles calls the shields Solomon's work; those object and provenance clauses remain distinct.

relationship: Bronze shield replacements and gateway runners with distinct actor clauses
rationale: Both make bronze shields in place of the earlier shields and mention gateway runners' commanders. Kings has the leaders place them on him; Chronicles says Sousakim appointed commanders over him. The actual agency and pronouns are not replaced with a shared custody procedure.

relationship: The king’s Lord-house entrance has runner or guard attendance
rationale: Both connect the king's entering the Lord's house with runners or guards. Kings specifies shields taken up and deposited in their chamber; Chronicles instead lists entering and returning groups without those shield-storage words.

relationship: Rehoboam’s closing record citations preserve different named sources
rationale: Kings cites the Annals of Judah's Kings for Rehoboam's remaining acts; Chronicles cites Samaia and Addo's records. These are corresponding regnal citation notices, not a claim that the cited works are the same recovered book.

relationship: Rehoboam-Jeroboam warfare is described as continual
rationale: Kings reports continual war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam; Chronicles likewise says Rehoboam fought Jeroboam all the days. The repeated pair and duration formula are retained without reconstructing every campaign.

relationship: The David-city burial and son’s succession close Rehoboam’s reign
rationale: Both bury Rehoboam with his fathers in David's city and name his succeeding son. Kings supplies Abiou and Chronicles Abijah; the parallel succession clauses do not independently normalize their personal forms.

relationship: Judah’s succeeding king begins in Jeroboam’s eighteenth year
rationale: Both place the new Judah reign in Jeroboam's eighteenth year. Kings names Abiou son of Rehoboam and Chronicles Abijah; the common accession framework does not change either supplied personal form.

relationship: The corresponding Judah regnal notices retain six versus three years and different maternal parentage
rationale: In the eighteenth-Jeroboam accession context, Kings gives six years and Maacah daughter of Absalom; Chronicles gives three years and Maacah daughter of Ouriel from Gabaon. The parallel regnal framework does not reconcile the duration or parentage.

relationship: Same-chapter The two royal heart assessments explicitly contrast incomplete and whole devotion
rationale: Abiou's heart is not whole with the Lord, whereas Asa's later assessment calls his heart whole all his days despite the high places. The contrast keeps the distinct kings and the qualifications actually stated.

relationship: David and Jerusalem provide the stated reason for a reserved continuation
rationale: Kings attributes a remnant, succeeding children and preserved Jerusalem to David's sake; the earlier promise reserves a share so David has a place in chosen Jerusalem. Remnant is not replaced with an absent lamp metaphor or a newly reconciled scepter count.

relationship: David’s command-keeping serves as an explicit royal model
rationale: The narrator gives David a right-conduct and command-keeping summary; the earlier divine condition likewise cites David's keeping commands and ordinances. The source's unqualified life summary is retained without inserting an absent exception clause.

relationship: The Abiou-Jeroboam war has a corresponding Abijah-Jeroboam notice
rationale: Kings names war between Abiou and Jeroboam; Chronicles names war between Abijah and Jeroboam in its regnal introduction. The matching war framework does not reconcile the different reign lengths or maternal statements elsewhere.

relationship: The king’s David-city burial is followed by Asa’s succession
rationale: Both close the preceding Judah king's reign with burial in David's city and Asa his son's succession. Kings' Jeroboam-year wording and Chronicles' ten-year quiet-land clause remain additional distinct statements.

relationship: Same-chapter Asa’s accession repeats the preceding succession notice’s date
rationale: The new heading makes Asa king in Jeroboam's twenty-fourth year; the preceding burial-and-succession notice gives the same year. Neither occurrence is replaced with another edition's familiar twentieth-year date.

relationship: Asa’s stated reign length and dated death preserve forty-one and thirty-nine
rationale: Kings gives Asa forty-one years in Jerusalem and names Ana as mother; Chronicles dates Asa's death to his thirty-ninth regnal year. The actual notices are compared without a corrected numeral, new co-regency or reconciled timeline.

relationship: Asa is assessed as doing right before the Lord
rationale: Kings says Asa did right before the Lord like David; Chronicles introduces his reign by saying he did good and right before his God. David's model remains the additional Kings clause rather than words inserted into Chronicles.

relationship: Asa removes condemned practices or abominations from the land
rationale: Kings removes initiatory rites and ancestral practices; Chronicles expels abominations from Judah, Benjamin and acquired cities. The actual labels remain distinct rather than identifying the rites as particular people or silently replacing them with another edition's wording.

relationship: The maternal removal and Kidron burning retain different names and objects
rationale: Kings removes Ana from leadership after a grove gathering and burns her hiding places at Kidron; Chronicles removes Maacah from Astarte ministry and burns an idol at Kedron. The named women, functions and destroyed objects are not independently equated.

relationship: Remaining high places coexist with the stated whole-heart assessment
rationale: Both keep a high-place nonremoval notice alongside Asa's whole or complete heart all his days. Chronicles explicitly locates its remaining high places in Israel; that geographical phrase is not supplied to Kings' shorter notice.

relationship: Silver, gold and vessels are brought into the Lord’s house with different object labels
rationale: Kings brings his father's and his own pillars—silver and gold pillars—and vessels into the Lord's house; Chronicles brings holy things with silver, gold and vessels. Pillars are not silently renamed holy things, and Chronicles' explicit David wording remains its own detail.

relationship: The Asa-Baasha conflict has a particular Ramah campaign account
rationale: Kings summarizes continual Asa-Baasha war; Chronicles describes Baasha attacking Judah and fortifying Rama against Asa. Its thirty-eighth-year date is not added to the general war summary or independently harmonized with every regnal notice.

relationship: Ramah construction is intended to block passage to Asa
rationale: Both describe Baasha fortifying Ramah or Rama to prevent going out and coming in for Asa. Their actual city forms and Chronicles' additional year remain intact rather than being converted into a new dated campaign reconstruction.

relationship: Silver and gold are sent to the son of Ader in Damascus
rationale: Both have Asa send silver and gold to the son of Ader, Syria's king in Damascus. Kings names the king-house treasury and additional ancestors; Chronicles also names the Lord-house treasury. Those provenance and patronymic details are not made identical.

relationship: The Asa-Syrian covenant request seeks Baasha’s withdrawal
rationale: Both ask a covenant involving the kings and their fathers, with gold and silver so Baasha departs. Kings specifically requests breaking a covenant with Baasha; that wording is not added to Chronicles' request to drive him away.

relationship: The son of Ader sends commanders against Israel in response to Asa
rationale: Both describe the Syrian king listening to Asa and sending commanders to attack cities including Dan and Naphtali's territory. Ain/Ion and Abelmaa/Abelmain and the remaining district forms are preserved without certifying every location equation.

relationship: Baasha abandons the Ramah building work after hearing the report
rationale: Both have Baasha hear and cease building Ramah or Rama. Kings additionally sends him back to Tirzah; Chronicles says he stopped the work, without that destination being inserted into its notice.

relationship: Ramah’s stones and timber are reused with different destination descriptions
rationale: Both accounts have Asa involve Judah and take Ramah's stones and timber for further building. Kings says the whole hill of Benjamin and watchtower; Chronicles names Gabae and Maspha. Those descriptions and the Ainakim extent are not independently normalized.

relationship: Asa’s foot illness occurs in the two closing reign accounts
rationale: Kings notes foot suffering in Asa's old age; Chronicles dates illness in his feet to the thirty-ninth year and adds its own Lord-and-physicians assessment. The comparison supplies no diagnosis or new timing to Kings' shorter notice.

relationship: Jehoshaphat the son succeeds Asa
rationale: Kings closes Asa's burial notice with Jehoshaphat his son reigning in his place; Chronicles opens the next account with Jehoshaphat his son becoming king. The preceding Asa death context identifies the paternal link without importing every burial detail.

relationship: Same-chapter Nadab’s accession and death are located in Asa’s second and third years
rationale: Kings gives Nadab two years beginning in Asa's second year; the later notice places Baasha's killing of him in Asa's third. The two actual dated notices are preserved without a new calendar or accession-year calculation.

relationship: Nadab’s Jeroboam-sin assessment recalls the named golden-heifer episode
rationale: Nadab follows his father's sin that caused Israel to sin; the Jeroboam account makes golden heifers, places them in Bethel and Dan, and calls the matter sin. The particular earlier narrative supplies context without reconstructing every later ritual.

relationship: Same-chapter The Gibbethon assault is followed by the explicitly named killing
rationale: Baasha attacks Nadab at Gibbethon during Israel's siege; the next unit expressly says Baasha put him to death and reigned. Belaan is retained as supplied rather than replaced with an unreported tribal ancestry.

relationship: Same-chapter Baasha’s reign begins in Asa’s third year in both notices
rationale: The killing-and-reigning notice dates Baasha's action to Asa's third year; his formal regnal heading gives that same accession year. The heading's twenty-four-year total is not independently reconciled with other later dates.

relationship: The named Jeroboam-house destruction corresponds to Ahijah’s stated word
rationale: Kings presents Baasha's destruction of Jeroboam's house as according to Ahijah's word; the earlier Ahijah speech announces destruction of Jeroboam's male household. The text's fulfillment claim does not independently approve every killing or identify every victim.

relationship: The Jeroboam provocation summary recalls the narrative explicitly called sin
rationale: The narrator explains the judgment by Jeroboam causing Israel to sin; the earlier golden-heifer narrative expressly says the matter became sin. This connects the stated grievance to its particular narrated worship arrangement without adding new ritual details.

relationship: Same-chapter Nadab’s annal citation belongs to the named earlier reign introduction
rationale: The closure cites Nadab's remaining deeds; the opening names Nadab son of Jeroboam with his Israel reign and its duration. This identifies the regnal subject without claiming the cited external annals were independently recovered or read.

relationship: Same-chapter The formal Baasha heading recalls the dated accession after Nadab’s death
rationale: Baasha son of Ahijah begins in Asa's third year; the earlier death notice likewise has Baasha kill and reign in that year. Tirzah and the twenty-four-year total remain the heading's additional data.

relationship: Baasha’s Jeroboam-way assessment is read beside the original sin episode
rationale: Baasha is said to follow Jeroboam's way and cause Israel to sin; Jeroboam's golden-heifer arrangement is the earlier narrative explicitly called sin. This does not invent an individual later ceremony or independently certify every participant's motives.

relationship: Same-chapter The Jehu-Hanani word introduction recurs in the extended charge
rationale: Both notices name Jehu son of Hanani, the Lord's speech and Baasha. The introduction says the word came to Baasha; the later notice expressly speaks against Baasha and his house, with additional reasons and an it clause whose object is not independently reassigned.

relationship: The divine leader-making claim concerns the named Baasha reign
rationale: The divine speech says Baasha was raised from the ground and made Israel's leader; the regnal heading names Baasha son of Ahijah as king over Israel. The attributed divine action and the narrator's accession data remain distinct statements.

relationship: Baasha’s threatened household is explicitly compared with Jeroboam’s destroyed house
rationale: The Lord's speech says Baasha's house will become like Jeroboam's; the earlier narrator reports Baasha destroying Jeroboam's house. The stated analogy is retained without solving the different agencies or supplying a new approval of the violence.

relationship: The city-dogs and plain-birds judgment formula recurs for another house
rationale: Baasha's city dead are assigned to dogs and plain dead to birds; the later Ahab-house statement uses the same city-and-plain division. The distinct royal households and speaker settings are not merged into one casualty account.

relationship: Baasha’s closing annal formula follows his named regnal heading
rationale: The closure cites Baasha's remaining acts and might; the earlier heading identifies his Israel reign in Tirzah. This links the regnal subject and record formula without claiming access to the cited Annals of Israel's Kings.

relationship: Same-chapter Elah son of Baasha and the Tirzah reign follow the burial notice
rationale: Baasha is buried at Tirzah and Elah his son succeeds; the next regnal unit names Elah son of Baasha reigning there for two years. The twentieth-Asa date is kept where stated rather than replaced with a familiar alternative.

relationship: Same-chapter The extended Baasha charge repeats the same named prophetic introduction
rationale: The later notice names Jehu son of Hanani and the Lord's charge against Baasha and his house; the opening introduces the Lord's word through that same named prophet to Baasha. The added hand-work and it clauses stay as supplied without independently deciding every object or motive.

relationship: Same-chapter Elah’s paternal and Tirzah identification corresponds to the succession notice
rationale: The heading gives Elah son of Baasha two years in Tirzah; the earlier notice names that son succeeding his buried father there. Their particular family and place data are compared without constructing a corrected regnal chronology.

relationship: Same-chapter The half-cavalry commander’s conspiracy is followed by the narrated strike
rationale: Zimri, commander of half the cavalry, conspires; the unit includes drinking in Tirzah at Osa's house, and the next unit names Zimri's striking, killing and succeeding. The drinking pronoun remains unassigned, cavalry is not changed into chariots, and no unreported weapon is added.

relationship: Same-chapter Zimri’s killing follows the named conspiracy and drinking scene
rationale: Zimri kills and reigns after the account of his conspiracy against the king in Tirzah. The preceding house-and-steward detail supplies the narrated setting without inventing an additional attack route or separate accomplice.

relationship: Same-chapter The Baasha-house destruction is read beside its particular threatened counterpart
rationale: Zimri strikes Baasha's entire house after taking the throne; the earlier Lord-speech announces action against Baasha and his house. The later event is linked to that specific threat rather than a new count or moral approval of victims' deaths.

relationship: Same-chapter The explicit Jehu-word fulfillment notice refers to the earlier oracle
rationale: The narrator says the event followed the Lord's word to Jehu; the opening names Jehu and states the Baasha-house judgment. This identifies the particular recorded word without inventing an additional oracle or treating every detail as independently reconstructed history.

relationship: Same-chapter The Baasha-Elah sin summary repeats the divine charge’s provoking language
rationale: The closure names Baasha and Elah's sins and uses causing-Israel-to-sin and worthless-things language; the earlier divine charge expressly addresses Baasha causing God's people to sin. The later singular causing-sin pronoun is not independently assigned to both men.

relationship: Same-chapter Elah’s annal closure belongs to the narrated Tirzah reign and attack
rationale: The citation names Elah's remaining acts after the narrative identifies his reign and Zimri's attack. Those canonical notices identify the subject without asserting that every deed in the cited annals has been read.

relationship: Same-chapter The Gibbethon camp receives the conspiracy news and appoints Omri
rationale: The short Zimri reign is placed beside Israel's Gibbethon camp; the next unit has that camp hear of the coup and make Omri king that day. The two king-making notices do not become a newly calculated reign chronology.

relationship: Same-chapter Omri’s camp appointment is followed by the Tirzah siege
rationale: The camp makes Omri the army commander king; the next notice has Omri and Israel go from Gibbethon to besiege Tirzah. Their named movement and action are retained without assigning every soldier an unreported allegiance motive.

relationship: Same-chapter The Tirzah siege is followed by the reported capture and fatal fire
rationale: Omri besieges Tirzah, then Zimri sees his city taken and burns the royal house over himself. The source's cave is preserved rather than replaced with a different palace structure or a new account of the fire's mechanics.

relationship: Same-chapter Zimri’s stated response follows the particular Tirzah siege
rationale: Zimri enters a cave of the king's house, burns the house over himself and dies after Omri's siege. The earlier siege supplies the narrated setting, without replacing cave with citadel or independently diagnosing his state of mind.

relationship: The Zimri assessment invokes the previously named Jeroboam sin pattern
rationale: The narrator attributes Zimri's fate to doing evil and walking in Jeroboam's sin; the earlier golden-heifer episode is explicitly called sin. The connection preserves the stated judgment without inventing a new ritual during his seven-day reign.

relationship: Same-chapter The conspiracy-annal formula follows Zimri’s particular narrated coup
rationale: The closure names Zimri's acts and conspiracies; the earlier account identifies his conspiracy, killing and accession. This connects a named regnal formula to its concrete narrative without claiming the external annals were recovered.

relationship: Same-chapter The two rival factions are followed by the stated outcome
rationale: Half the people support Thamni and half Omri; the next unit gives Omri's faction the advantage and records Thamni and his brother Joram dying. The additional Joram notice is retained rather than removed from the succession account.

relationship: Same-chapter The outcome names the same rival support groups
rationale: Omri's supporters overpower Thamni's after the prior division between those two candidates. The deaths and brother relation stay in the outcome unit, without identifying this Joram with later kings of that name.

relationship: Same-chapter Omri’s Tirzah regnal phase precedes the named hill-building account
rationale: The heading gives Omri twelve years, six in Tirzah; the next unit records acquiring and building the Semeron hill. The unassigned remaining years are not automatically placed in a reconstructed city chronology.

relationship: Same-chapter Omri’s named hill-building account beside his Samaria burial notice
rationale: Omri buys Shemer's hill and names the hill he built on Saemeron; the later closure buries Omri in Samaria. The particular hill-building and burial sequence retains Semeron, Saemeron and Samaria without a newly certified place equation or modern map.

relationship: Same-chapter Father and son receive the explicit worse-than-predecessors assessment
rationale: The narrator says Omri did worse than all before him; Ahab's later assessment repeats that comparative judgment. The two named kings remain distinct, and the comparison does not independently rank every individual act.

relationship: Omri’s Jeroboam-way charge refers to the earlier named sin arrangement
rationale: Omri follows Jeroboam's way and causes Israel to sin; the earlier narrative locates the golden heifers in Bethel and Dan and calls the matter sin. The link does not add an unreported later cult inventory.

relationship: Same-chapter Omri’s closing acts formula is read with the particular narrated building deed
rationale: The annal citation names Omri's remaining acts and might; the earlier account gives his hill acquisition and building. It provides a recorded canonical deed without claiming it exhausts the cited annals or all his accomplishments.

relationship: Same-chapter Ahab son of Omri follows Omri’s burial and succession notice
rationale: Omri's closure names Ahab his son succeeding him; the later Ahab regnal heading again identifies Ahab son of Omri, after the intervening Jehoshaphat continuation block. The heading's Jehoshaphat-year and reign length stay in their own statement.

relationship: Jehoshaphat’s thirty-five-year accession and twenty-five-year reign notices correspond
rationale: Both give Jehoshaphat thirty-five at accession and twenty-five years in Jerusalem. Gazouba daughter of Selei and Azouba daughter of Sali remain the respective maternal forms; no new personal-name equation or regnal chronology is established.

relationship: The Asa-way assessment and remaining high places appear in both Jehoshaphat summaries
rationale: Both say Jehoshaphat follows Asa's way and does right, while high places remain. Chronicles adds its people-heart statement; that clause is not imported into Kings or used to erase the different notices of reform elsewhere.

relationship: Jehoshaphat’s regnal record citations name different sources and scopes
rationale: Kings cites the Annals of Judah's Kings for agreements, might and wars; Chronicles names Jehu son of Anani's accounts and a Kings of Israel book. The cited works are not independently identified as one volume or claimed recovered.

relationship: The son’s remaining-unions removal is read beside Asa’s earlier removal notice
rationale: Jehoshaphat removes remaining unions from the land from Asa's days; Asa's earlier account removes initiatory rites and ancestral practices. The related father-and-son removal notices retain the different terms without a new identification of the practices or people involved.

relationship: Same-chapter The Syria-nasib notice stays within the explicitly headed Jehoshaphat account
rationale: The original no-king-in-Syria and nasib notice occurs within the expanded Jehoshaphat regnal block; its opening names Jehoshaphat and his reign. This supplies the actual literary frame without changing Syria to Edom or independently translating nasib.

relationship: Jehoshaphat’s unsuccessful ship project has a parallel with distinct destinations and partnership clauses
rationale: Kings' single Tarshish ship for Sophir's gold is wrecked at Ezion-geber; Chronicles has ships built at Gasion-gaber and reports their wrecking and inability to go to Tharsis. The singular/plural, destination, building-place and alliance notices are preserved without a single reconstructed voyage.

relationship: The unwillingness and reported partnership remain different shipping notices
rationale: Kings' unnamed Israel king offers attendants and young men aboard the ship, but Jehoshaphat is unwilling; Chronicles names partnership with Ahaziah for ship construction. Those statements are compared without assigning the anonymous king a name or declaring the offer accepted.

relationship: Jehoshaphat’s David-city burial and Joram’s succession correspond
rationale: Both bury Jehoshaphat with his fathers in David's city and name Joram his son reigning in his place. The parallel clauses do not merge that son with the earlier brother of Thamni who also bears Joram's name.

relationship: Same-chapter The named Ahab-Omri father-son succession receives its formal regnal heading
rationale: The heading names Ahab son of Omri reigning in Samaria; the earlier closure names Ahab as the son succeeding Omri. Its second-Jehoshaphat-year and twenty-two-year data are not silently replaced with familiar alternative dates.

relationship: Same-chapter Ahab repeats the earlier Omri comparative evil assessment
rationale: Ahab is said to act more wickedly than all before him; Omri had received the same worse-than-predecessors assessment. The repeated narrative formula is compared without making the two lives or deeds identical.

relationship: Jezebel’s marriage notice relates to the later table-associated prophets
rationale: Kings introduces Ahab's wife Jezebel and his Baal service; Elijah's later gathering request names prophets who eat at Jezebel's table. The specific royal-cult setting is linked without inventing a new count of confirmed attendees or assigning every prophet identical support.

relationship: Same-chapter The Baal altar follows the named Baal-service notice
rationale: Ahab places a Baal altar in the house of offenses built in Samaria after the account of serving and bowing to Baal. The connection follows the named worship and altar without replacing the supplied house title.

relationship: Same-chapter The grove and provocation notice continues the royal cult-building account
rationale: Ahab makes a grove after the Baal-altar and house notice; the narrator then gives its extended provocation assessment. The grove is not independently placed inside that house or relabeled as a different specific cult object.

relationship: The firstborn-foundation and youngest-gate curse is explicitly recalled
rationale: Kings connects Hiel's Jericho building with Joshua's word, naming Abiram and Segub; Joshua states the foundation-and-gates curse and adds Ozan's example with Abiram. Hiel/Ozan and the named or unnamed younger-son clauses remain distinct rather than independently harmonized.

relationship: Elijah’s multi-year no-rain announcement has an explicit later prayer summary
rationale: Kings has Elijah announce no dew or rain these years except through his word; James names Elijah praying for no rain and gives three years and six months. The prayer and quantified duration are not inserted into Kings' initial speech.

relationship: Same-chapter The word introduction receives its specific hiding-and-provision content
rationale: The Lord's word comes to Elijah and then directs him to Chorrath with water and commanded ravens. The introduction is tied to that actual message rather than an unspecified later oracle.

relationship: Same-chapter The Chorrath instruction is followed by residence at the named place
rationale: The instruction sends Elijah eastward to hide at Chorrath facing the Jordan; the next action notice says he follows the word and stays there. It does not independently describe an unreported concealment procedure.

relationship: Same-chapter The raven-and-wadi provision promise has its stated outcome
rationale: The word promises wadi water and ravens sustaining Elijah; the narrator later gives bread in the morning, meat in the evening and wadi drinking. Those different morning/evening foods are not merged into two identical meals.

relationship: Same-chapter The named residence corresponds to the actual Chorrath directive
rationale: Elijah acts according to the word and stays at Chorrath facing Jordan; the earlier command names that place and direction. The report is not expanded into unmentioned observers, journeys or a new modern location.

relationship: Same-chapter The particular supplied food and water answer the prior provision statement
rationale: Ravens bring morning bread and evening meat while Elijah drinks from the wadi; the promise names raven sustenance and wadi water. It does not place both bread and meat in each time slot.

relationship: Same-chapter The wadi’s drying is expressly attributed to the absence of rain
rationale: The narrator says the wadi dries because rain has not fallen; Elijah's opening speech announces no rain during these years except through his word. The connection preserves the narrated cause without adding a rainfall total or exact duration.

relationship: Same-chapter The renewed word introduction leads to the particular widow-provision command
rationale: The Lord's word again comes to Elijah, followed by the Zarephath direction and widow provision. This attaches the formula to its particular recorded content without treating the earlier raven instruction as unchanged.

relationship: Elijah’s Sidonian Zarephath widow is explicitly recalled by Jesus
rationale: Kings directs Elijah to a widow in Zarephath in Sidonian territory; Luke explicitly says Elijah was sent to a widow at Zarephath in Sidon's territory. The named location, prophet and recipient are retained without an added widow's personal name.

relationship: Same-chapter The Zarephath journey and widow encounter follow the stated direction
rationale: Elijah goes to Zarephath and encounters a wood-gathering widow at the gateway after the word directs him there. The actual encounter does not supply an unreported earlier conversation with the widow or a different destination.

relationship: Same-chapter The bread request receives the widow’s specific scarcity reply
rationale: Elijah asks for bread as the widow goes for water; she replies with no hearth cake and only flour and oil. Her we-will-eat-and-die expectation remains her speech rather than an independently confirmed outcome.

relationship: Same-chapter The stated flour-and-oil scarcity is answered by the nonexhaustion promise
rationale: The widow describes a handful of flour and little oil for herself and children; the Lord-word promises that flour and oil will not diminish. The water jar and plural children remain as supplied rather than familiar substituted vessel or household forms.

relationship: Same-chapter The food-preparation direction is followed by action and eating
rationale: Elijah directs the widow to prepare food for him and then herself and children; the narrator says she acts and she, he and her children eat. It does not independently enumerate every serving step or an additional number of days.

relationship: Same-chapter The flour-and-oil promise is expressly reported fulfilled
rationale: The Lord-word promises the flour jar will not be exhausted and oil will not diminish; the later notice repeats those outcomes according to the word through Elijah. The rain endpoint remains in the promise rather than an invented elapsed period.

relationship: Same-chapter The woman’s action and household eating follow the actual preparation directive
rationale: The woman acts and she, Elijah and her children eat after his direction to prepare food. The narrator's order of listed eaters is not turned into an independently confirmed serving order or a many-days statement absent here.

relationship: Same-chapter The repeated nonexhaustion wording refers to the earlier explicit promise
rationale: The narrator attributes undiminished flour and oil to the Lord's word through Elijah; that word had specified those same two provisions. Their particular containers and wording remain unchanged rather than a generic claim about every famine.

relationship: Same-chapter The breathless child’s illness is followed by Elijah’s son-lives declaration
rationale: The child becomes severely ill until no breath remains; the later account returns him to his mother with Elijah's declaration that her son lives. The comparison adds no independent diagnosis or medical mechanism.

relationship: Same-chapter The widow’s accusation is followed by Elijah’s differently addressed complaint
rationale: The widow accuses Elijah of bringing her wrongdoings to remembrance and putting her son to death; Elijah then addresses the Lord with a harm-and-death complaint. These remain distinct speakers' attributions rather than a new narrator's cause-of-death verdict.

relationship: Same-chapter Taking the child upstairs is followed by bringing him down to his mother
rationale: Elijah takes the boy from the woman's bosom to his upper-room bed; he later brings him down and returns him to the mother. The matching movement-and-return sequence does not add an unreported helper or place.

relationship: Same-chapter Elijah’s complaint and the widow’s prior blame retain their respective addressees
rationale: Elijah cries to the Lord and attributes the widow's harm and son's death to Him; the widow had blamed Elijah. The two spoken accusations are compared without rewriting either into a question or independently adjudicating their claims.

relationship: Prophetic prayer and bodily acts concerning a child have distinct forms and counts
rationale: Elijah breathes into the child three times and prays for his soul's return; Elisha prays, lies upon the child and bends over him as many as seven times. The different actors, movements, counts and reported responses are not merged into one procedure.

relationship: Same-chapter The brief cried-out result follows the particular soul-return prayer
rationale: After Elijah breathes and prays for the child's soul to return, the narrator says it happened so and the child cried out. The actual brief result is retained without inserting an additional quoted response from the Lord.

relationship: A restored son is given back to his mother in the two narratives
rationale: Elijah brings the child down, gives him to his mother and declares him living; Luke has the formerly dead young man speak and Jesus give him to his mother. The particular maternal return is shared without assigning identical bodily acts or prayer wording.

relationship: Same-chapter The woman’s recognition follows the returned living son and Elijah’s declaration
rationale: The woman acknowledges Elijah as a man of God whose Lord-word is true after he returns her son and says he lives. The response is connected to that particular narrated exchange without inventing a different sign or an added name for the woman.

relationship: The rain promise and renewed Ahab meeting follow the earlier no-rain announcement
rationale: The Lord tells Elijah to show himself to Ahab and promises rain; Elijah had earlier announced no rain except through his word. The third-year notice is preserved without an independently reconciled interval against other summaries.

relationship: Same-chapter Elijah’s going to Ahab follows the explicit show-yourself command
rationale: Elijah goes to show himself to Ahab after the Lord directs that meeting. The famine-severity statement remains part of the action notice rather than an unprovided numerical measure of drought or deaths.

relationship: Same-chapter Obadiah’s Lord-fear assessment corresponds to his own rescue report
